catalog_citation: Hamilton, R.C. 1900. An Outline Grammar of the Dafla Language as spoken by the tribes immediately south of the Apa Tanang country. Shillong: Assam Secretariat Printing Office. (archive.org anoutlinegramma01hamigoog)
catalog_locator: Part I, sec. III 'Accent', printed p. 2 (PDF page 18 of the archive.org scan; page scan saved)
catalog_quote: III.—Accent. In the Dafla language accent does not apparently play so important a part as in Miri. The accent usually falls on the penultimate syllable of a word, but in delivering a sentence the position of a word in such sentence may cause it to change its accent or even to change its vowels from long to short or vice versâ, in order to suit the cadence of the sentence, e.g., Iki mûllûngâ chê-û-sû-dna. Dog (plural) biting together are. } The dogs are fighting. but— Lûpâ au-nâm iki-a* si. Neck (in) shot been dog this. } This is the dog that was shot in the neck. In the former sentence 'iki' is rather slurred over, but in the latter it is the most important word, and a slight pause takes place before pronouncing it, which has the effect of lengthening the first vowel and shortening the second. [* Nominatival 'a'.]

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Hamilton 1900 passage is verbatim on the page scan we hold (printed p.2, sec. III 'Accent', p.18) and in the scanned text we hold; citation and locator are correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1900 colonial officer's outline grammar (grammar sketch). It is the only work seen that says anything about word accent in Nyishi, and what it says is hedged (accent matters little; position shifts with sentence cadence; vowel length changes under focus). All later material we hold or downloaded today (CIIL LIS-India, Rimum 2021, Goswami 1995 p.3, Post 2015 p.190/Table 5, Dey 2017, Gogoi et al. 2026) describes Nyishi in terms of tone (three tones per CIIL/Rimum; 'conflicting reports' per Post, who could not detect tone in Lower Nyishi) and is silent on stress, so nothing contradicts the penult coding but nothing modern supports it either. (3) The works that could supersede Hamilton

tone.quote: Phonemic tone is found in most relatively well-described Tani languages, including Apatani (all dialects), Galo (all dialects), Na/Bangni, Upper Minyong and Tangam, as well as in Milang. … In the case of underlying morphemes, no more than two contrastive tones have been attested for any Tani language: an unmarked H and a marked L. … At least some Tani languages or dialects thereof seemingly lack lexical tones, including Lower Adi, Mising and Nyishi. Unfortunately, due to an ongoing lack of adequate description (particularly of ET languages), reconstruction of PT tone categories is problematic.

sources.note: Branch survey: tone not prevalent in Tani; lexical pitch to varying degrees in Western Tani (Nishi-Bengni, Hill Miri); one Na Bengni variety has high vs low on some words, another uses vowel quality.

tone.quote: Phonemic tone is not a prevalent feature. While completely non-existent in such eastern languages as Bokar, lexically significant pitch occurs to varying degrees in many Western languages. In one type of Na Bengni, for example, high-low pitches need to be lexically marked for certain words, e.g. taH-nuO L ‘hemp’, taL-nuO H ‘snail’. In another Bengni dialect, interestingly, the same words are distinguished by vowel qualities: ta-noO ‘hemp’, ta-nuO ‘snail’.
